proposals.name: Standing converted into otherwise-unavailable operational facts
proposals.instruction: Score how far the commenter's stated position in the regulated world is actually cashed out as facts an outsider could not obtain. 10: the comment names a concrete role with respect to the regulated activity (operator, obligated party, service provider to the affected population, sovereign, practitioner) AND then reports position-specific particulars that follow from that role -- counts of facilities, internal procedures, caseload experience, what happens to clients, market share, which equipment is in which fleet, what the commenter's staff must do. 5: a clear and specific stake is identified but everything offered afterward is publicly available background or general advocacy. 0: the writer's relationship to the rule is unstated, or is present only as mission/credential language with no role-specific facts anywhere in the text. Judge the conversion, not the prestige of the affiliation.
proposals.rationale: R44 (FedEx names six clearance locations under 19 CFR 128 handling thousands of import shipments daily, then reasons from that) and R01 (Legal Aid reports what its clients actually encounter -- Treasury offset of public benefits, tax-refund offset, administrative wage garnishment on MTF debts) both spend their standing; R30 does the same as a named obligated party with a specific refinery. By contrast R16 and R25 carry full institutional letterhead, a named executive, and a docket citation but convert none of it into facts, and R09 devotes most of its visible text to a mission narrative whose particulars are about the organization rather than about what the rule does. A scorecard reading for 'identifies affected interests' credits all of these equally; this criterion separates them.

proposals.name: Names a specific defect in the agency's reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment locates a particular flaw in how the agency got to its proposal, as opposed to disagreeing with the result. 10: the comment identifies a specific mismatch and shows why it is a mismatch -- the rule's operative text does not track the purpose the agency stated, the stated rationale does not reach the cases the rule will actually govern, the record does not support an inference the agency drew, or the agency's own account of its constraints is internally inconsistent. 7-8: a real defect is named but the demonstration is thin. 3-4: general dissatisfaction with the proposal's direction, with the agency's reasoning left untouched. 0: the comment accepts the agency's framing entirely, or expresses a preference with no engagement of any reasoning at all.
proposals.rationale: R02 shows the statute defined 'transit bus' by use while defining over-the-road buses physically, so physically identical buses fall on opposite sides of a rule whose purpose is physical rollover risk -- a defect in fit, not a preference. R07 shows EPA's rationale is driven by energy-infrastructure projects while the rule will govern water storage and supply projects that are 'very different', so the justification does not reach the governed cases. R10 turns EPA's own posture against it (if past guidance had been adequate Congress would not have directed a rule). R39 shows the 'currently occupied habitat' definition defeats the recovery purpose it is supposed to serve. Against these, R21 and R17 accept the agency's framing wholesale, and R43 endorses a rationale it restates in the agency's own terms.

proposals.name: Adds material to the record the agency did not have
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the comment puts new information into the docket. 10: the comment identifies specific evidence, studies, documents, datasets, or historical agency statements that it represents as absent from or unaddressed by the agency's record, and says what they show. 6-7: it supplies real evidence, but evidence the agency plainly already has. 3: it gestures at evidence existing without identifying it. 0: it contains no evidence beyond the commenter's opinion, or its citations point back at the agency's own proposal and guidance documents. Reciting the agency's sources back to the agency scores at the low end no matter how formally the citations are formatted.
proposals.rationale: R15 explicitly offers '40 relevant sources not discussed in the original listing decision, final 4(d) rule, and the recent species status assessment' and asks that they be included; R39 supplies post-2013 population discoveries with citations (Bergamini et al. 2017, Woods et al. 2018) that postdate the record; R08 excavates a 1969 agency statement, a 1992 IIHS admonition, and 2013 academic work on undercounting; R40 notices that a new docket does not contain its 2013 comments and resubmits them. The contrast is R53, whose formal reference list points at FDA's own 1992 policy statement plus an unrelated cell-based-meat article, and R45, whose figures are widely circulated general statistics. Citation apparatus is easy to score for; net addition to the record is not.

proposals.name: Legal authority is load-bearing, not decorative
proposals.instruction: Score whether cited statutes, regulations, cases, or legislative history do argumentative work. 10: an authority is quoted or paraphrased accurately and an inference is drawn from it that changes what the agency may or must do -- the rule exceeds a grant of authority, a provision compels a different reading, a decision constrains the analysis the agency owes. 5: authorities are cited accurately and relevantly but only to establish background or the commenter's eligibility to comment. 2: citations, links, or section numbers appear as ornament, attached to claims they do not support. 0: no authority invoked, or authority invoked incorrectly.
proposals.rationale: R48 argues the proposed rule 'is not authorized by the Commodity Promotion, Research, and Information Act of 1996, 7 U.S.C. 7411-7425' and adds that the Secretary already holds plenary oversight under 7 C.F.R. 1206.70, so the rule is both ultra vires and unnecessary -- two conclusions drawn from the sources. R07 quotes CWA 101(b) and 510(1) and builds the cooperative-federalism argument out of the quoted words. R40 cites Weyerhaeuser to support a particular exclusion and invokes ESA 4(b)(2) as the vehicle. Against these, R42 attaches federalregister.gov paragraph links to questions it does not answer, and R53 name-checks the FD&C Act without deriving anything. A criterion bank that rewards 'cites legal authority' cannot tell these apart.

proposals.name: Adoption-ready remedy joined to its justification
proposals.instruction: Score the pair, not either half. 10: the comment states a change the agency could adopt substantially as written -- specific regulatory text to amend, a number, a threshold, a definition, a severance of the rulemaking -- AND the reason that change follows from the commenter's analysis. 7: a precise remedy with only asserted justification, or a well-justified position whose remedy is left for the agency to construct. 3: a directional preference ('do less', 'act quickly') with neither text nor reasons. 0: no requested action, or only questions posed to the agency.
proposals.rationale: R50 writes the amendment ('Amend Prop. Treas. Reg. Sec. 1.861-18(f)(2)(ii) to more clearly state that ...') after setting up why the current text misfires. R30 gives four numbered actions carrying actual quantities (13.8 billion gallons; at least 390 million and at least 1.2 billion gallons) each tied to a stated consequence. R02 asks for a narrow definitional refinement and spends the letter earning it. R13 proposes bifurcating the rulemaking and supplies the reason (H-1B cap season begins in about two months). At the other end R60 lists what it opposes and asserts 'current limits ... should stand' with no reasons, R36 asks for 'NO action' on sentiment, and R42 supplies only questions. Remedy specificity alone is cheap; the joint is what is rare.

proposals.name: Payload density: share of text doing argumentative work
proposals.instruction: Estimate what fraction of the comment's body actually advances a claim about the proposal, as against self-description, letterhead, rosters, boilerplate mission statements, tables of contents, headings without text under them, transmittal formalities, and pointers to material not included. 10: nearly everything present is argument, evidence, or a requested change; institutional framing is brief and subordinate. 5: roughly half the visible text is apparatus or self-description. 0: the text is essentially apparatus -- an outline, a membership list, a mission narrative, or a cover note -- with the argument absent, promised elsewhere, or never begun. Score the text present, not the document it implies.
proposals.rationale: R26 is a table of contents whose headings ('USFWS PROVIDES A MISLEADING DISCUSSION', 'INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE') advertise analyses that never appear in the text; R23 is largely a roster of Stakeholder member agencies plus 'generally support'; R09 spends its length on organizational mission and general background; R16 is a transmittal plus a scheduling request. A scorecard scanning for analytic headings, formal structure, and identified interests reads R26 and R23 as thoroughly organized. Meanwhile R37 and R19 carry almost no apparatus at all -- no letterhead in R19 -- and are argument end to end.

proposals.name: Independent analysis versus restatement of the proposal
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the comment could NOT have been written by someone paraphrasing the notice. 10: the comment's substance consists of evaluations, consequences, mechanisms, or facts brought from outside the proposal; any summary is compressed and in service of a point. 5: an accurate and useful summary with a modest evaluative overlay. 2: the proposal is reproduced provision by provision with agreement or approval appended to each. 0: the text is a paraphrase of the agency's own materials with approving adjectives and no independent content.
proposals.rationale: R17 reproduces the proposed trip limits, seasons, and allocations species by species with 'DSF Agrees with these proposed changes' appended to each block -- near-total restatement wearing the surface of detailed technical engagement. R21 accurately summarizes the APHIS user-fee methodology and adds little evaluation. R53 summarizes FDA's own guidance documents back to FDA and calls the collection 'essential'. Compare R06, which restates the ULSD/heating-oil redesignation mechanics only in order to interrogate them, and R13, whose summary is compressed to make room for consequences. Restatement is highly correlated with every surface marker of specificity, which is exactly why a criterion bank over-credits it.

proposals.name: Calibrated two-sided stance with reasons for each side
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment distinguishes among the parts of the proposal on stated grounds. 10: it identifies what is sound and what is not and gives the reason for each judgment, so the agency learns where the disagreement actually lies. 6: the stance is uniform but the reasoning is specific enough to show it was reached rather than assumed. 3: uniform approval or disapproval carried by adjectives. 0: undifferentiated praise, undifferentiated condemnation, or imputation of bad faith to the agency in place of argument.
proposals.rationale: R13 states 'The proposal contains many positive developments', names them (start-date flexibility, deference codification, entrepreneur eligibility), and only then enumerates the provisions its members regard as harmful. R39 opens with 'kudos to the US Fish and Wildlife Service staff' and 'impressive' documentation before mounting a sustained critique of the occupancy limitation. R18 and R31 both separate what they support from what they contest. Against these, R32 imputes bad faith throughout ('purposely doing a fake study', 'pushed by lobbyists') while the real scope objection buried inside it goes undeveloped, and R43 and R45 are uniform endorsements. Two-sidedness is a strong signal that the commenter actually read and weighed the proposal, and it is not the sort of thing a per-property criterion bank catches.

proposals.name: Offers a fallback if the primary request is refused
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment anticipates being turned down and gives the agency something usable anyway. 10: it states a primary position and then an explicit conditional alternative ('if the agency nevertheless proceeds, then ...'), or offers two independent routes to the relief sought, or proposes a different means to the agency's own stated goal. 5: an alternative is hinted at without being specified. 0: a single categorical demand with no second-best, or no request at all.
proposals.rationale: R18 urges retention of the 2020 Rule and then says 'If, however, EPA chooses to move forward with the Proposed Rule, these comments suggest revisions to reduce the risk of re-creating or exacerbating the problems resolved by the 2020 Rule.' R44 states that 'there are alternate methods of achieving the goals laid out in this proposal', accepting the agency's objective and contesting only the means. R40 gives two independent grounds (no designation along Eagle Creek; alternatively exclusion under Section 4(b)(2) based on existing management plans). R13 proposes bifurcation as a way to salvage the urgent piece. R36 and R60, by contrast, present one categorical demand. This shape of cooperativeness is legible to a careful reader and invisible to a property checklist.

proposals.name: Traceable chain from provision to concrete consequence
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment walks a mechanism from a specific feature of the rule to an identified effect on identified parties. 10: each link is stated and plausible -- this provision produces this behavior, which produces this cost, delay, exposure, or harm, falling on these people. 6: the endpoint harm or benefit is concrete but the intermediate steps are asserted. 3: a vague claim of burden or benefit with neither mechanism nor affected party specified. 0: values, sentiment, or conclusions with no causal content.
proposals.rationale: R01 runs the chain end to end: patients rarely choose which emergency department receives them, MTF debts have no financial-assistance path, those debts go to Treasury for offset of public benefits, tax refunds, and wage garnishment, and the result is measured against 'basic needs of survival'. R44 traces fee-announcement timing to clearance delays to higher costs ultimately borne by consumers. R57 runs volumes above the blendwall through vehicle warranty and infrastructure incompatibility to supply disruption. R13 links the cap-season calendar to employers' inability to plan. Against these, R36 asserts that habitat 'must be protected, not disrupted and destroyed' without a mechanism, and R41 states a need without connecting it to any provision.

proposals.name: Empirical claims are attributed and checkable
proposals.instruction: Score the sourcing discipline of the comment's factual assertions. 10: quantitative and empirical claims carry identifiable sources (agency report numbers, named surveys, named datasets, dated studies) and the cited source plausibly supports the specific claim made. 6: sources are named loosely (an agency, an organization) but locatable. 3: figures and findings are asserted with no attribution, or attributed only to 'researchers' or 'studies'. 0: unattributed claims are compounded with speculation the commenter flags as guesswork. Judge the linkage between claim and source, not the quantity of numbers.
proposals.rationale: R08 footnotes its fatality and cost figures to specific documents (NHTSA DOT HS 813 435, FMCSA RRA-22-007, the BLS inflation calculator, IIHS); R22 sources its smoking-prevalence contrast to the 2021 NSDUH detailed tables with a URL and defines the survey's terms; R47 attributes the 62.9% average volume share to USDA's Global Agricultural Trade System. Compare R11, which reports a 'significant warming trend', a 1C decadal rise, 0.5C nighttime warming, and work by 'David Keith and colleagues' and 'Vautard' with no retrievable citation, then closes with 'maybe this is why bad storms in tex this year'; and R45, whose 50%, 25%, and one-third figures float free. R11 and R45 present many of the surface features of evidence, which is precisely the trap.

proposals.name: Private interest translated into the agency's public criteria
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment connects what the commenter wants to the considerations the agency is actually charged with weighing. 10: a self-interested ask is expressed in terms of the statutory factors, the rule's stated purpose, or effects on parties beyond the commenter -- safety, cost to consumers, supply reliability, program integrity, the interests of the wider regulated class -- and the connection is argued rather than asserted. 6: the public dimension is named but the argument stays about the commenter. 2: the ask is purely about the commenter's own convenience, paperwork, or schedule. 0: the comment asks for an accommodation and offers no reason the agency should care beyond the commenter's preference. Being self-interested is not penalized; failing to translate it is.
proposals.rationale: R30 recasts its own cost relief as the Clean Air Act factors EPA must consider (infrastructure, cost to consumers, cost to transport goods, job creation) and argues EPA weighed them wrongly. R57 frames the blendwall as a consumer and fuel-supply problem. R31, an industry association, supports the reading that narrows an exemption and grounds it in 'the millions of Americans who will share the road'. R47 argues board representation should track the promotional revenue its members generate, in the interest of 'producers, marketers, retail establishments, and the end consumers alike'. Against these, R49, R38, and R59 seek changes to their own compliance paperwork and applicability lists with no account of why the public interest turns on it.

proposals.name: Individually composed rather than templated or duplicated
proposals.instruction: Score whether the text was written for this proposal by this writer. 10: the reasoning is specific to the writer's situation and could not be dropped into another docket -- particular incidents, particular role conflicts, particular operations. 6: individually written but generic in content. 3: recognizable campaign or form language, stock framings, or a signature block indicating a mass-submission channel. 0: the comment duplicates its own text (a 'background' section reproducing the opening verbatim), or consists of standard talking points with only a name attached. Do not reward or punish length or formatting; look for whether the sentences were built for this rule.
proposals.rationale: R19 arrives with no letterhead at all and is unmistakably individual -- it argues from what CAP staff specifically must know (Rehabilitation Act rights, ADA advocacy, the need to consult attorneys on fact-specific cases) and why merging their training with VR counselor training creates conflicting purposes. R37 does the same work with a concrete instance of its CAP program advocating against state VR policy. R34 grounds its safety argument in a named co-founder nearly struck on a Montana shoulder in 2014. Against these, R27's 'Background' paragraph reproduces its opening paragraph nearly word for word beneath a campaign signature block, and R45 and R12 read as circulated talking points. Institutional polish and individual authorship are different things, and a criterion bank tends to measure the first.

proposals.name: Command of the rule's history and prior record
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment situates the proposal in its own regulatory lineage. 10: it accurately traces what came before -- prior rules and what problems they were meant to solve, prior agency commitments or statements, related dockets, the commenter's own earlier submissions, statutory enactments and their sequence -- and uses that history as part of the argument. 5: history is mentioned but does not bear on the claim. 0: the proposal is treated as if it appeared from nowhere, or the comment shows no awareness that the question has been visited before.
proposals.rationale: R18 explains that the 2020 Rule replaced regulations not substantially revised since before the 1972 CWA enactment, what problems that gap created, and asks EPA to consider whether the new proposal would resurrect them. R08 assembles a 54-year record of inaction from a 1969 agency statement anticipating side underride protection through a 1992 IIHS admonition to the IIJA mandate. R40 notes that the Service opened a new docket that does not contain its 2013 comments and resubmits them so they are not overlooked -- history as procedural risk. R03 grounds its reading in the 2005 and 2007 enactments and congressional intent. Against these, R28 supports deleting a recordkeeping requirement with no account of why it exists, and R43 endorses a realignment on generic efficiency grounds.

proposals.name: Contested consequential question versus ministerial housekeeping
proposals.instruction: Score what kind of question the comment engages. 10: it takes up something genuinely at issue in the rulemaking -- the agency's authority, the scope of a right or obligation, who bears a cost, whether the evidentiary basis supports the action -- where reasonable parties disagree and the agency must choose. 5: a real but bounded implementation question with material consequences. 2: an internally uncontested correction: a typographical error, a figure reference, an applicability list, a compliance-date alignment, a schedule extension. 0: a procedural request needing no substantive content at all. High precision on a small question is not the same as engaging a large one; score the question, not the precision.
proposals.rationale: This is the largest single pattern in the card-high half. R49 corrects station numbers and part counts in service-bulletin figures; R59 asks that three engine models be removed from an applicability list; R29 asks that two compliance windows be harmonized; R38 asks that an airworthiness limitation be relocated from one NPRM to another; R33 asks which service bulletin should be mandated. All are precise, docket-cited, technically fluent, and internally uncontested -- exactly the profile that scores well on specificity and expertise criteria. R16 and R25 are extension requests with no substantive content whatever. Compare R56 (whether EPA may rescind methane limits), R07 (the scope of state authority under Section 401), and R48 (whether the Department may remove commodity board members) -- questions the agency cannot dispose of by correcting a figure.

proposals.name: Scan and OCR degradation artifact density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of optical-character-recognition and page-conversion damage visible in the text. Count as damage: words split one letter per line or stacked vertically; substituted glyphs (e.g. '£' where 'f' belongs, '~', '(cid:9)', 'V/' for 'W'); missing spaces between words joined by scanning; stray isolated digits or page numbers on their own line; column or table content flattened into a vertical run of numbers and fragments; every line of a paragraph separated by a blank line. 0 = clean, continuously readable text with no conversion damage. 5 = frequent glyph substitutions or blank-line shredding but sentences remain reconstructable. 10 = large stretches are unreadable rubble of stacked characters and orphaned numbers. Score only how MUCH damage is present. Do NOT judge whether the damage is bad, whether it makes the comment worse, or whether the underlying content is good or poor.
proposals.rationale: This is a property of the ingestion pipeline (image PDF vs. digital PDF vs. typed-in-box), not of the writer's argument. R05 and R12 are near-total OCR rubble (vertically stacked letters, 'flet' for 'fleet', 'witha'), R21 is a 1980 typewritten scan where every 'f' reads '£', and R32 carries mangled address glyphs; meanwhile R03 has clean words but every line is blank-line separated. A text model can easily learn to key on this signature, but it tracks how the document was digitized, not what it says.

proposals.name: Attachment-transmittal stub preceding the substantive body
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item is fronted by a transmittal stub whose only function is to point at an attached file. Look for opening lines such as 'See attached file(s)', 'See Attached', 'Please see attached', 'Comments from X are submitted herewith', 'Attached please find', a bare leading '0' or '1', and the run of blank or whitespace-only lines that follows before real prose begins. Score higher when such a stub is present, longer, repeated, or followed by many empty lines; score 0 when the item begins directly with substantive prose and contains no pointer-to-attachment language. Score only the presence and size of the stub. Do NOT judge whether using an attachment is appropriate, professional, or good.
proposals.rationale: The stub records the submission mechanism (uploaded document plus a cover note) rather than any property of the argument. R06 and R35 open with a bare 'See attached file(s)' and blank lines before an institutional letter; R30 and R57 do the same; by contrast R02, R38 and R42 are typed straight into the web form and carry no stub at all. The marker separates two upload pathways that cut across the whole quality range.

proposals.name: Sheer bulk and running to the excerpt cutoff
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of raw textual bulk. Anchor on how far the item runs and whether it terminates mid-sentence or mid-word at a hard cutoff rather than at a natural close. 0 = a few sentences that end with a complete closing (a short request or question). 3 = one or two full paragraphs, cleanly ended. 6 = roughly a page of prose that still closes naturally. 10 = a long run of text that is still in mid-argument, mid-sentence, or mid-word when it stops, with no closing or signature reached. Score length and truncation only. Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the writer is thorough, or whether long is better than short.
proposals.rationale: Pure verbosity proxy, deliberately included as a nuisance so it can be discounted. R03, R33 and R52 run to the cutoff and break off mid-sentence ('Private, working fores', 'proposes several changes to the'), while R02, R19 and R38 are three-to-five-sentence submissions that close cleanly. Any scorer reading only the text can pick this up trivially, and it is confounded with document type rather than with what is argued.

proposals.name: Orthographic noncompliance and unedited-typing residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of departures from standard written-English mechanics: misspelled or transposed words ('theri', 'probalby', 'producgts', 'Wom'), missing apostrophes ('cant', 'Its been', 'isnt'), missing or doubled spaces around punctuation, sentences beginning in lower case, run-on sentences joined without punctuation, inconsistent capitalisation of ordinary words (e.g. shouting a common noun mid-sentence), and stray unclosed parentheses or quotation marks. 0 = no such departures. 5 = several per paragraph but the text is still easy to follow. 10 = departures in nearly every sentence. Count occurrences and score the density only. Do NOT judge whether the writer is careless, uneducated, sincere, or whether the mechanics make the comment better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Mechanics track whether anyone proofread the keystrokes, not whether the point is sound. R10 is dense with typos and missing apostrophes throughout, R55 mixes shouted words ('WIND', 'WILDLIFE') with a dropped-space run-on, R40 opens 'To Wom It May Concern' and writes 'nowbut', and R01 has 'Its been' and 'cant' inside an otherwise conventional letter. The feature is highly visible to any text model and is orthogonal to whether the underlying request is well grounded.

proposals.name: Alphanumeric part, docket and service-bulletin identifier density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text is populated by dense alphanumeric technical identifiers: part numbers, model or engine designations, service-bulletin and airworthiness-directive numbers, revision and issue numbers, station or figure/table/step references, standard codes with mixed letters, digits and hyphens (e.g. 'V2527E-A5', 'BACB30NX6K3', '737-71-1937 RB', 'STA 1233', 'FMVSS No. 227', 'Prop. Treas. Reg. Sec. 1.861-18(f)(2)(ii)'). Count how many distinct such strings appear and how large a share of the sentences carry at least one. 0 = none. 5 = several per paragraph. 10 = identifiers dominate, with most sentences built around them. Score density only. Do NOT judge whether the identifiers are correct, relevant, or whether their presence indicates expertise.
proposals.rationale: This is a subject-matter marker for a specific docket genre (aviation airworthiness and technical-standard corrections), not a measure of merit. R49, R51, R59 and R26 are built almost entirely from such strings, and R12 carries them through heavy OCR noise, whereas R40, R53 and R54 contain none. A scorecard keyed on specificity-looking tokens and a dense reader will diverge on exactly this genre, so the token pattern itself must be declared a nuisance.

proposals.name: Legal-authority citation and case-law formatting density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of formal legal-authority citation apparatus in the text. Count: Federal Register cites ('85 Fed. Reg. 23608'), U.S. Code and C.F.R. cites ('33 U.S.C. Sec. 1341', '49 C.F.R. Sec. 571.227'), public-law and statute-section cites, reported case citations with reporter and year ('139 S. Ct. 361, 368 (2018)'), 'see', 'citing', 'pursuant to', 'Id.', numbered footnotes carrying full source references, and quoted statutory language set in quotation marks. 0 = no citation apparatus at all. 5 = a handful of statutory or Federal Register cites. 10 = citation apparatus is continuous, with cases, statutes and footnotes threaded through most paragraphs. Score the amount of citation machinery only. Do NOT verify the citations, and do NOT judge whether citing authority makes the comment stronger.
proposals.rationale: Whether the drafter had legal training is unobservable, but it leaves the citation apparatus as a fingerprint. R39 (State of Colorado) and R36 (New Flyer) thread U.S.C., C.F.R. and public-law cites through every paragraph, R30 cites Weyerhaeuser with pinpoint pages, and R52 carries statutory footnotes, while R38, R42 and R47 raise comparable regulatory points with no apparatus whatsoever. Tagged mixed because trained counsel plausibly also improves the substance, so this channel must appear in the sensitivity band rather than being discounted outright.
proposals.upstream_parent: access to legal training or counsel when drafting

proposals.name: Representational-mandate and constituency-size self-description
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text devotes space to describing the submitter's organisation, its membership and whom it speaks for. Count: explicit member or constituent counts ('more than 620 corporate members', 'over 30,000 professional flight crewmembers', 'more than 13,800 dermatologists', 'approximately 250 U.S. business enterprises'), founding dates and longevity claims, lists of member categories or named member entities, superlatives of scope ('the oldest and largest', 'the world's largest'), and 'on behalf of' framing that enumerates the represented parties. 0 = no self-description of the submitter. 5 = a single sentence or short paragraph of organisational description. 10 = one or more full paragraphs, or an itemised roster of represented entities, before or alongside the substance. Score how much such self-description is present. Do NOT judge whether the organisation is important, credible, or whether representing many people should matter.
proposals.rationale: Organisational scale is not visible to a text-only model except through this boilerplate paragraph, which is exactly where it leaves its trace. R33 (API, '620 corporate members'), R35 (CAPA, '30,000 professional flight crewmembers'), R45 (ASSE, '37,000' plus a full board roster), R14 (AADA, '13,800 dermatologists') and R27 (an itemised list of stakeholder districts and cities) all carry it; R16, R42 and R47 carry none. Tagged mixed because a large, well-resourced association may also genuinely produce better-supported comments.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional resources, membership scale and network of the submitter

proposals.name: Outside-firm production stamps and prepared-for/prepared-by markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of artifacts showing the document was produced through a professional document-production workflow. Count: document-management or matter-tracking codes ('EAST\164420197.2', '{00609.002 / 111 / 00204871.DOC 2}'), network or drive file paths embedded in the text ('Q:\Jobs\1000's\1049.142\...'), explicit 'Prepared for:' / 'Prepared by:' blocks with a firm name and project number, named law or consulting firms appearing as the author or in the letterhead, 'Managed by ... Consortia Management' style service-provider lines, formal tables of contents with dotted leaders and multi-level numbered sections, and 'Page N of M' running headers repeated across pages. 0 = none of these. 5 = one or two such markers. 10 = several distinct markers, including an internal tracking code or file path plus a firm-authored front matter block. Score presence and count only. Do NOT judge whether professional preparation makes the comment better.
proposals.rationale: Retaining a firm is an unseen resource fact, but it leaks into the text as production residue. R08 carries a raw network file path plus 'Prepared for: Rosemont Copper Company / Prepared by: WestLand Resources, Inc.' and a dotted-leader table of contents; R60 carries the document-management stamp 'EAST\164420197.2'; R43 carries '{00609.002 / 111 / 00204871.DOC 2}' and a consortium-management line; R24 and R30 are authored on law-firm letterhead. Tagged mixed because paid preparation plausibly raises genuine substance as well as leaving this signature.
proposals.upstream_parent: engagement of paid outside counsel or a consulting firm to prepare the submission

proposals.name: Procedural posture about deadlines, extensions and prior filings
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text is occupied with the mechanics of the comment process rather than with the content of the rule. Count: requests to extend or reopen the comment period; statements about how long the comment period was or when it closes; complaints that the available time was insufficient; notices that the submitter previously commented, is resubmitting, or fears earlier comments were lost when a docket was renumbered; references to a related or parallel rulemaking whose schedule interacts with this one; and requests that the agency bifurcate, sequence or expedite its rulemakings. 0 = no process content. 5 = a paragraph of process content alongside substantive discussion. 10 = the item is essentially a procedural request with little or no discussion of the rule's merits. Score how much process-mechanics content is present. Do NOT judge whether the procedural request is reasonable or well founded.
proposals.rationale: The conjectured parent is the agency's own calendar and docket handling, which does not make a submitter's substantive analysis any better or worse, yet it leaves an unmistakable textual fingerprint. R18 (Philip Morris) and R58 (ACC Center for Biocide Chemistries) are pure extension requests keyed to a 90-day window and a holiday-season deadline; R13 complains that 'the one month comment period provided for this proposed rule is much too short'; R30 explains it is resubmitting 2013 comments because the Service opened a new docket; R27 notes prior comment letters on two earlier drafts.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and process dynamics on the receiving side (comment-period length, docket renumbering, calendar conflicts)

proposals.name: Coordination and campaign-participation fingerprints
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of textual signs that the submission is part of a coordinated effort rather than independently composed. Count: explicit endorsement of or concurrence with another party's already-filed comment ('I concur with the supporting comments posted by ...'); transmitting or appending a parent, national or affiliate organisation's comment letter as the substance; a campaign or advocacy-staff sender identity in the signature or email header (role-based addresses such as campaign.rep@..., subject lines formatted as a stock position plus a docket number); recurring stock talking-point phrasing paired with a personal sign-off; and a jointly filed submission listing several allied organisations as co-signers. 0 = no such signs. 5 = one clear sign, such as appending an affiliate's letter or a role-based campaign sender. 10 = multiple signs, e.g. stock phrasing plus explicit concurrence plus campaign-staff identity. Score the visible coordination markers only. Do NOT judge whether coordination is legitimate, whether the position is popular, or whether a coordinated comment deserves more or less weight.
proposals.rationale: Mobilisation is an organisational fact upstream of the text, and it shows up as these residues. R34 states outright that the writer 'concur[s] with the supporting comments posted by the NWPB's President and Vice President'; R15 forwards the National Corn Growers Association's letter as its own substance; R22 is sent from a role address, campaign.rep@nyc.surfrider.org, with the subject 'Dissent for EPA-HQ-OW-2019-0405-0025'; R01 pairs a personal family narrative with stock nutrition-label campaign lines ('More realistic serving sizes would better reflect what we are likely to eat'). Tagged not-mixed because a recruiting campaign drives who files, not how substantively sound the filing is.
proposals.upstream_parent: organised mobilisation by an association or advocacy campaign that recruits and templates submitters

proposals.name: Developed multi-step reasoning chain vs bare assertion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment builds an explicit chain of reasoning: a claim followed by supporting premises, evidence, or sub-arguments that connect logically to that claim across multiple sentences or paragraphs. Score 0 if the comment merely asserts a position, preference, or conclusion with no supporting reasoning chain at all. Score in between based on how many linked reasoning steps are present.
proposals.rationale: R04 (Gov. Inslee's letter) and R33 (Truck Safety Coalition) each build extended, multi-paragraph reasoning chains connecting evidence to a conclusion, while R29 and R55 state strong positions/emotional appeals with little to no developed reasoning chain.

proposals.name: Legal/regulatory-authority argumentation citing specific provisions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment cites specific statutory sections, regulations, or case law and argues how those authorities constrain, permit, or conflict with the proposed action, integrating the citation into a substantive legal argument. Score 0 if the comment shows no engagement with legal or regulatory authority whatsoever.
proposals.rationale: R52 (State of Colorado) builds a sustained cooperative-federalism argument citing specific Clean Water Act sections, and R27 (National Mango Board) argues the proposal exceeds authority under the Commodity Promotion Act and its implementing order; R01 similarly cites Weyerhaeuser v. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Serv. with a pincite.

proposals.name: Direct rebuttal of agency's stated rationale
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment identifies a specific claim, finding, or justification stated by the agency in the proposal (paraphrased or quoted) and directly rebuts it with counter-evidence or counter-reasoning. Score 0 if the comment does not engage with the agency's own stated reasoning at all.
proposals.rationale: R04 directly rebuts EPA's justifications for rolling back methane standards, and R33 quotes the agency's own 1969 statement about extending underride protection and uses it against the agency's decades of inaction.

proposals.name: Precision of requested regulatory text edit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment identifies a precise textual or provision-level change (a specific paragraph, defined term, list entry, or figure) and states exactly what should replace or be removed from it. Score 0 if the comment expresses only a general sentiment about the rule with no specific textual change identified.
proposals.rationale: R11 (New Flyer) asks NHTSA to revise the specific 'transit bus' definitional language, and R26 (International Aero Engines) asks that section '(c) Applicability' be revised to remove three named engine models by part number.

proposals.name: Policy rationale depth behind technical correction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a specific technical or procedural request is accompanied by an explanation of its underlying purpose, safety rationale, or downstream consequences if not adopted. Score 0 if the comment states only the technical fact or correction itself with no explanation of why it matters.
proposals.rationale: R11 extends its transit-bus correction into a lengthy discussion of legislative intent and comparative rollover-risk safety rationale, whereas R42 (Qantas) and R26 (IAE) state precise corrections with comparatively little discussion of broader purpose beyond compliance logistics.

proposals.name: Evidentiary specificity: concrete checkable facts
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment supplies multiple specific, checkable facts (statistics with sources, named prior dockets or documents, dates, quantities) that support its claims. Score 0 if the comment contains no concrete, checkable facts, only vague or general assertions.
proposals.rationale: R33 cites specific footnoted NHTSA statistics (5,700 deaths, a 71% increase since 2009, $66 billion in losses), and R51 (Dr. Nowak) cites named studies and specific populations (Woods et al. 2018, Bergamini et al. 2017) supporting its claims.

proposals.name: Declared subject-matter expertise or firsthand experience
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the writer explicitly identifies personal or professional expertise, credentials, or firsthand operational experience directly relevant to the specific subject matter, and visibly draws on that experience in the argument. Score 0 if no expertise or experiential basis for the claims is stated anywhere in the text.
proposals.rationale: R51 (Dr. Nowak) grounds its critique in '20+ years of research with Thamnophis rufipunctatus,' and R13 (UPS Airlines) grounds its correction in firsthand knowledge of exactly which seat models are installed on which of its aircraft fleets.

proposals.name: Evaluative critique vs descriptive restatement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment is overwhelmingly evaluative -- it takes a position on specific elements of the proposal and gives reasons for or against them, spending little space merely restating the proposal or the commenter's own background. Score 0 if the comment is almost entirely descriptive or explanatory, restating the rule or the commenter's identity without evaluating or critiquing specific provisions.
proposals.rationale: R58 (NAMC/NMA) is pointedly critical of the proposal's lack of specificity and argues the point, while R08 (South Dakota Cattlemen's Association) spends most of its space describing the proposed fee mechanism and the commenter's role rather than evaluating specific provisions.

proposals.name: Explicit structural organization of distinct points
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment uses explicit structural devices -- headings, numbered or lettered points, an executive summary, or roman-numeral sections -- to separate and label multiple distinct arguments or requests. Score 0 if the comment is an undifferentiated block of prose with no structural markers separating distinct points.
proposals.rationale: R03 (Monroe Energy) opens with an 'EXECUTIVE SUMMARY' header and a bulleted list of specific requested actions, and R11 (New Flyer) organizes its argument with roman-numeral and lettered sub-headings ('I.', 'A.').

proposals.name: Formal address to decision-maker as submission
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text is explicitly framed and formatted as a formal submission addressed to the named agency or official, with a docket/RIN citation, salutation, and a closing that identifies the submitter and their role. Score 0 if the text reads as an informal, conversational note or internal exchange (e.g., first-name address, casual sign-off) not framed as an address to the decision-maker.
proposals.rationale: R59 (Lapointe's internal peer-review email, 'Mike - I'm not sure what you need here... Aloha, Dennis') is informal and internally addressed despite substantive technical content, in contrast to R51's formally captioned docket comment addressing a closely related listing decision.

proposals.name: Textual coherence vs OCR/scanning degradation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text is clean, fluent prose free of scanning artifacts or non-prose fragments. Score 0 if the text is dominated by garbled OCR errors, broken or misspelled words, or disconnected numeric/table fragments that impede reading the underlying argument.
proposals.rationale: R13 (UPS Airlines) and R43 (Calleguas Creek Stakeholders) are heavily degraded by OCR errors ('flet' for 'fleet', 'ltr/ater' for 'Water'), and R02 is dominated almost entirely by raw chart-extracted numbers with virtually no connected prose.

proposals.name: Density of quantitative/numeric data content
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment is saturated throughout with specific quantitative figures (dollar amounts, percentages, counts, or time series). Score 0 if the comment contains no numbers or quantitative figures at all. Score based purely on the presence and density of numeric content, independent of whether it appears in connected prose.
proposals.rationale: R02 consists almost entirely of extracted numeric/chart data (funding percentages and dollar figures across 2002-2017), and R33 also supplies dense quantitative content ('5,700 lost their lives,' 'increase of 71%,' '$66 billion') woven into its narrative.

proposals.name: Narrow focus on one well-defined issue
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment identifies and stays tightly focused on one specific, well-defined issue or discrepancy throughout its entire length. Score 0 if the comment wanders across many loosely related topics or offers only generic, unfocused commentary spanning several unrelated issues.
proposals.rationale: R32 (Jetstar) stays entirely focused on specific STA-figure and parts-count discrepancies in one service bulletin, and R25 stays focused on a single interpretive question about how contingent restitution orders are reported under Section 6050X, in contrast to broader multi-issue letters like R17 (U.S. Chamber), which spans H-1B registration, F-1 flexibility, and the 'specialty occupation' definition in one letter.

proposals.name: Personal stake and lived-experience narrative
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment describes a specific personal situation, need, or lived experience that concretely motivates the requested action (e.g., a named health condition, a specific caregiving situation, a specific disability-related need). Score 0 if the comment contains no personal narrative or stated personal stake, reading as a generic or impersonal statement.
proposals.rationale: R24 (Nancy York) grounds its request for updated Nutrition Facts labels in her husband's heart condition and her family's struggle with obesity, and R31 grounds its request for accessible public transportation in the commenter's own identification as a person with LD and specific mobility needs.

proposals.name: Acknowledgment and response to counter-considerations
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the comment explicitly acknowledges a competing interest, cost, trade-off, or plausible counterargument to its own position and responds to it. Score 0 if the comment presents a purely one-sided case with no acknowledgment of any competing consideration.
proposals.rationale: R28 (National Hydropower Association) explicitly weighs the problems the prior rule solved against the risks of the new proposal and offers fallback revisions 'if... EPA chooses to move forward,' and R17 (U.S. Chamber) explicitly separates the NPRM's 'positive developments' it supports from the provisions it opposes rather than rejecting the whole proposal.

proposals.name: Overall length and verbosity of the submission
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (extremely brief, a sentence or two) to 10 (very long, multi-page with extensive elaboration), rate how much text/verbosity this item contains. Judge ONLY the raw quantity of words and elaboration present, not whether the length is appropriate, wasteful, or improves the argument. Do not judge whether the comment is well- or poorly-argued.
proposals.rationale: Row R43 is an extended multi-page data dump of tables/figures while R15, R26, and R29 are one- or two-sentence comments; length is plausibly driven by how much staff time/resources a producer could devote to drafting rather than by argument quality itself, a well-known length confound in text-based scoring.

proposals.name: Presence of a generic 'see attached' transmittal phrase
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no generic transmittal phrase present) to 10 (the item opens with, or consists largely of, a stock phrase such as 'See attached file(s)', 'Please see attached comments', or similar, before or instead of substantive content), rate how much of the item is this kind of boilerplate submission-portal phrasing. Score only the presence/extent of this stock phrase, not whether the underlying attachment (if any) is good.
proposals.rationale: R01, R04, R08, R10, and R44 all open with a near-identical 'See attached file(s)'/'Please see attached' stub before the real letter; this is an artifact of the regulations.gov submission portal and PDF-attachment extraction pipeline, not of the argument's substance.

proposals.name: Degree of OCR/scanning garbling in the text
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (clean, modern digitally-typed text with no recognizable scanning errors) to 10 (heavily garbled with OCR artifacts: misrecognized letters, broken words, stray symbols, reversed characters), rate how much OCR/scan-quality garbling is visible in the text. Score only the visible garbling, not whether the underlying argument is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('heolfh industry monufQcfurers QSSOCfQtlon') and R34 ('bhe External Peer Review... Woter Quality') show heavy OCR garbling typical of older/scanned filings, while recent electronic filings like R08 or R38 are clean; garbling reflects the age/format of the original filing pipeline, not the quality of the argument.

proposals.name: Extent of formal organizational letterhead/footer elements
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no letterhead elements; plain body text only) to 10 (extensive letterhead/footer block with organization name, mailing address, phone/fax numbers, and/or website URL), rate how much formatted organizational letterhead or footer material appears in the item. Score only the presence and extent of these formatting elements, not whether the organization or its letterhead looks professional or credible.
proposals.rationale: R05 (South Dakota Cattlemen's Association, PO Box/phone header) and R13 (American Petroleum Institute, full address/phone/fax/email/website block) carry dense letterhead blocks that individual commenters like R15 or R29 never have; letterhead density tracks organizational resources for professional formatting, which could bias a reader independent of the argument's merit.

proposals.name: Density of formal legal/regulatory citations
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no formal citations) to 10 (frequent precise citations to case law, U.S.C./C.F.R. sections, or Federal Register pin-cites, e.g. '87 Fed. Reg. 16442' or 'Weyerhaeuser v. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Serv., 139 S. Ct. 361, 368'), rate how much formal legal/regulatory citation apparatus is present. Score only the extent of citation apparatus present, not whether the cited authorities are used correctly or persuasively.
proposals.rationale: R06 cites 'Weyerhaeuser v. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Serv., 139 S. Ct. 361, 368 (2018)' and precise Federal Register pin-cites, and R23/R33 similarly cite C.F.R./Federal Register sections extensively; this citation apparatus is a textual fingerprint of professional legal drafting/editing resources, which could be favored independent of the underlying argument's soundness.

proposals.name: Explicit self-identification of professional title/credentials
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no title, degree, or professional affiliation given) to 10 (signature block explicitly states a formal title, academic degree, and/or institutional affiliation, e.g. 'PhD', 'Senior Vice President', 'Assistant Research Professor'), rate how much explicit credentialing/title information the commenter provides about themselves. Score only whether such self-identification is present in the text, not whether the stated credentials are impressive or relevant.
proposals.rationale: R08 signs as 'Erika M. Nowak, PhD, Assistant Research Professor, Northern Arizona University' and R13 signs as 'Frank J. Macchiarola, Senior Vice President, Policy, Economics and Regulatory Affairs', while R09, R15, and R29 give only a first name or no title at all; explicit credentialing is a textual signal of the author's stated seniority that a reader could weight independent of argument quality.

proposals.name: Extent of stated coalition/membership backing
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no membership or coalition claim; single named individual) to 10 (item explicitly states it represents, or is submitted jointly on behalf of, multiple organizations or a large membership, e.g. 'representing more than 270 companies' or 'joined ... by'), rate how much explicit collective/institutional backing is claimed in the text. Score only whether such a claim is present and how prominent it is, not whether the claimed membership size is true or whether it makes the argument correct.
proposals.rationale: R02 (HIMA, 'representing more than 270 companies'), R13 (API, 'more than 620 corporate members'), and R18 (NAMC and NMA jointly) foreground large claimed constituencies, while R09, R15, and R26 are single unaffiliated individuals; stated coalition size is a textual fingerprint of network/resource backing that could sway a reader independent of the argument itself.

proposals.name: Reference to prior submissions or ongoing history with the agency
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no reference to any prior interaction with the agency or docket) to 10 (item explicitly references having previously submitted comments, resubmits earlier comments, or otherwise describes an ongoing history of engagement with this agency/rulemaking), rate how much the text signals prior engagement/repeat-player status. Score only whether this kind of reference is present in the text, not whether the commenter's history makes their current argument more correct.
proposals.rationale: R06 (Freeport) explicitly states it 'previously submitted comments on the agency's first critical habitat proposal' and is 'resubmitting its 2013 comments', and R34 (Calleguas Creek Stakeholders) states it 'previously submitted a comment letter on the External Peer Review Draft'; this repeat-player fingerprint could bias a reader toward familiar, experienced filers regardless of the current comment's substance.
proposals.upstream_parent: process experience / repeat-player status with the agency

proposals.name: Extent of generic mobilization-campaign phrasing
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (phrasing reads as an individually composed, idiosyncratic statement) to 10 (phrasing follows a generic advocacy-campaign template, e.g. opens with a formulaic 'I strongly SUPPORT/OPPOSE the proposed rule...' or a bare imperative like 'Please [add/keep] X...' with no personal detail specific to the commenter), rate how much the text resembles templated mass-mobilization language rather than an individually composed statement. Score only the presence of this templated phrasing pattern, not whether the position taken is correct or well-reasoned.
proposals.rationale: R40 opens with 'I strongly SUPPORT the proposed critical habitat protections...' and R24 opens with 'I'm opposed to the suggested, across-the-board increase...', both formulaic position-statement openers typical of organized campaign talking points, distinct from more idiosyncratic short comments like R27's list of open questions; campaign-templated phrasing reflects mobilization-drive participation, not the individual's own substantive contribution.

proposals.name: Presence of tabular/numeric data blocks vs. continuous prose
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (entirely continuous prose, no tables or numeric listings) to 10 (item consists substantially of tables, columns of figures, part-number/station listings, or other non-prose data blocks), rate how much of the item's text is structured as tabular/numeric data rather than prose sentences. Score only the extent of this formatting pattern, not whether the underlying data is accurate or relevant.
proposals.rationale: R43 is dominated by long runs of dollar-figure and percentage data extracted from a chart, and R12 lists STA (station) numbers and part numbers in a bulleted technical table; this reflects the source document's genre/format (financial exhibit, engineering bulletin) rather than the substantive quality of the comment's argument.

proposals.name: Actionable Textual Precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies exact provisions, locations, or wording and supplies a precise corrective change; score 0 when it offers only a general position without text-level specificity.
proposals.rationale: Motivated by the highly specific amendment requests in R14, R16, and R31, contrasted with broad requests in other comments.

proposals.name: Causal Consequence Chain
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment clearly traces a provision through an operational mechanism to concrete effects on identified parties; score 0 when it asserts benefits or harms without explaining how they arise.
proposals.rationale: R13 and R30 connect regulatory details to refinery, energy, licensing, and environmental consequences rather than merely stating opposition.

proposals.name: Objective-Preserving Alternative
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment proposes a workable alternative that addresses the stated regulatory concern while preserving the underlying public-purpose objective; score 0 when it offers no alternative or only asks for withdrawal.
proposals.rationale: R14, R23, and R32 suggest narrower, better-targeted implementation approaches instead of merely objecting.

proposals.name: Applied Legal Reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment accurately applies statutes, regulations, or precedent to specific provisions and explains the resulting interpretive issue; score 0 when legal authorities are absent or merely listed.
proposals.rationale: R20, R36, and R44 use statutory language and case law to analyze agency authority and proposed changes.

proposals.name: Quantified Empirical Support
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment presents relevant numerical evidence with identifiable sources, definitions, and context; score 0 when factual claims are unsupported, purely anecdotal, or unquantified.
proposals.rationale: R15, R37, and R45 provide concrete volumes, rates, fatalities, emissions, and cited data sources.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Domain Insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment explains specialized technical, scientific, or clinical mechanisms linking conditions to effects; score 0 when it relies on conclusions, slogans, or generalized concern without domain explanation.
proposals.rationale: R26 explains habitat fragmentation and species ecology, while R40 and R51 discuss disease transmission and atmospheric mechanisms.

proposals.name: Adaptive Ongoing Support
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies changing conditions and specifies recurring training, monitoring, guidance, or revision needed over time; score 0 when it treats a complex issue as requiring only a one-time action.
proposals.rationale: R24 and R56 emphasize continuing technical assistance, legal updates, and case-specific support; R23 similarly addresses evolving maintenance documentation.

proposals.name: Cross-Document Consistency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies conflicts, duplication, or mismatched terminology across related rules, standards, service bulletins, or documents and proposes a coherent resolution; score 0 when it examines only one isolated text.
proposals.rationale: R14, R23, R28, and R31 identify overlapping aircraft requirements, inconsistent documents, and duplicated compliance obligations.

proposals.name: Conditional Edge-Case Analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment tests the provision against multiple contingencies or borderline cases and explains how each should be handled; score 0 when it addresses only an uncomplicated default case.
proposals.rationale: R19 analyzes contingent restitution outcomes, R17 probes definitional and participation edge cases, and R28 considers overlapping installation timelines.

proposals.name: Firsthand Stakeholder Exposure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the commenter connects its position to concrete firsthand experience, affected populations, operations, or recurring cases; score 0 when organizational identity is asserted without describing actual exposure to the issue.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R58 describe repeated legal-service encounters with medical debt, while R11 explains dermatologists’ direct clinical experience.

proposals.name: Balanced Issue Appraisal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment fairly acknowledges useful features or competing considerations and then distinguishes them from specifically supported concerns; score 0 when it is entirely conclusory, one-sided, or disconnected from the proposal’s details.
proposals.rationale: R01, R02, and R57 acknowledge beneficial or sound elements before explaining targeted reservations and tradeoffs.

proposals.name: Research Integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment synthesizes prior submissions, studies, surveys, or technical literature into a cumulative argument and explains their relevance; score 0 when references are absent or appended without integration.
proposals.rationale: R09, R26, R29, and R40 build on earlier submissions, published studies, and accumulated technical research.

proposals.name: Implementation Feasibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment addresses how affected parties would comply in practice, including timing, records, staffing, sequencing, or transition arrangements; score 0 when it discusses policy merits without implementation details.
proposals.rationale: R14, R23, R28, and R54 focus on compliance timing, fee predictability, records, and operational continuity.

proposals.name: Systematic Proposal Coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment methodically addresses multiple relevant provisions or questions and distinguishes support, concerns, and recommendations for each; score 0 when it gives only a broad position or isolated example.
proposals.rationale: R01, R25, and R55 organize comments across numerous provisions, species, transactions, or regulatory subtopics.

proposals.name: Equity-Specific Impact Analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies a particular burden or benefit for vulnerable, underserved, or differently situated groups and proposes a concrete way to address it; score 0 when it invokes fairness or public benefit without identifying affected groups or mechanisms.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R58 analyze low-income patients’ medical-debt burdens, while R24, R27, and R47 identify disability and health-access implications.

proposals.name: Institutional branding
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much visible organizational branding, letterhead, office information, websites, or logos appear; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Formal organizational markers are visible in R05, R58, and R60, and may affect apparent authority or processing independently of substantive content.

proposals.name: Credential display
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the text visibly states author titles, degrees, senior roles, professional designations, or years of experience; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Explicit credentials appear in R03, R54, and R58, potentially signaling status independently of the comment's substantive content.

proposals.name: Coalition representation
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the text visibly claims to represent members, clients, companies, communities, coalitions, or multiple submitting organizations; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Representation claims are prominent in R18, R24, R53, and R60, and may signal network reach independently of the text's substantive quality.

proposals.name: Legalistic citation register
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much formal legal phrasing, statutory citations, case citations, regulatory provisions, and numbered legal arguments appear; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Dense legal registers appear in R08 and R50, potentially signaling professional assistance or institutional familiarity independently of substantive content.

proposals.name: Production layout polish
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much visible pagination, section hierarchy, tables of contents, repeated headers, footnotes, graphics, or polished document formatting appears; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Highly produced layouts appear in R10, R47, and R58, and may affect readability or apparent formality independently of the underlying substance.

proposals.name: Document bulk and verbosity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the visible amount of prose, pages, sections, tables, appendices, references, or repeated elaboration; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: The very different document scales visible in R10 and R22 can predict processing burden or attention without measuring substantive quality.

proposals.name: Template boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much stock docket language, submission formulas, repeated courtesy phrases, attachment notices, or standardized organizational wording appears; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Formulaic language appears in R01, R45, and R49, potentially reflecting coordinated production independently of the comment's substantive content.

proposals.name: Timing and urgency cues
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the text visibly emphasizes deadlines, comment-period dates, prompt action, immediacy, upcoming seasons, or time pressure; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Urgency and deadline language appears in R44, R51, and R56, and can reflect timing circumstances rather than substantive quality.

proposals.name: OCR and transcription artifacts
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much visible character substitution, broken spacing, scanning noise, malformed symbols, missing letters, or transcription error appears; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Conversion artifacts are visible in R15, R31, and R49, potentially affecting apparent polish or readability without reflecting the underlying content.

proposals.name: Technical identifier density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much specialized model numbers, part numbers, docket codes, scientific names, acronyms, units, or alphanumeric identifiers appear; do not judge whether this feature is good, bad, persuasive, or substantively valuable.
proposals.rationale: Identifier-heavy language appears in R09, R13, and R27, providing topic or venue signals independent of substantive quality.

proposals.name: Regulatory Issue Targeting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment accurately identifies several specific provisions, definitions, or requirements in the proposal and addresses them directly; score 0 when it offers only generic approval, opposition, or unrelated discussion.
proposals.rationale: R03, R26, R32, and R46 engage particular sections, figures, or statutory mechanisms, whereas R01 and R59 remain largely general.

proposals.name: Actionable Amendment Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment supplies concrete, text-level changes that an agency could implement, such as replacement language, deletions, carve-outs, or revised deadlines; score 0 when it requests change without specifying what should change.
proposals.rationale: R03, R26, R43, and R48 identify precise revisions, while R28 and R59 mainly express support or opposition.

proposals.name: Cross-Rule Consistency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies interactions, overlaps, or contradictions among related rules, standards, guidance, or service documents and explains how to reconcile them; score 0 when it treats the proposal in isolation.
proposals.rationale: R06, R18, and R32 identify duplicative or conflicting aircraft requirements, while R04 and R29 do not develop comparable regulatory interactions.

proposals.name: Evidence Traceability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when important factual claims are tied to identifiable studies, datasets, statutes, cases, technical documents, or named sources; score 0 when claims are unsupported or impossible to trace from the text.
proposals.rationale: R02, R12, R19, and R30 connect arguments to numerous identifiable sources, unlike R14 and R17, which make broad factual assertions without usable provenance.

proposals.name: Quantitative Reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment uses relevant quantities, comparisons, trends, or calculations and explains how they bear on the proposal; score 0 when numbers are absent or presented without interpretation.
proposals.rationale: R19, R24, R30, and R60 use numerical evidence to connect the proposal with industry, health, safety, or economic effects, whereas R01 and R59 provide no comparable analysis.

proposals.name: Causal Mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment clearly traces how a proposed provision would change conduct or conditions and thereby produce specific effects for people, organizations, markets, or ecosystems; score 0 when it merely asserts that the proposal is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R11, R31, R39, and R49 explain concrete pathways from regulatory design to access, debt, health, or environmental consequences, while R04 and R28 mostly state expected benefits.

proposals.name: Implementation Feasibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment addresses how regulated parties or agencies would administer, comply with, document, monitor, or enforce the proposal in practice; score 0 when practical execution is not discussed.
proposals.rationale: R18, R32, R54, and R60 discuss compliance records, timing, fee administration, or operational burdens, while R17 and R35 do not address implementation mechanics.

proposals.name: Legal Authority Analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies relevant statutes, regulations, or precedents and applies their language or structure to the specific proposal; score 0 when legal authority is absent or invoked only as a conclusory slogan.
proposals.rationale: R13, R16, R46, R53, and R25 interpret statutory text, precedent, or delegated authority, while R01 and R59 contain no comparable legal analysis.

proposals.name: Boundary-Case Testing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment tests the proposal against multiple concrete edge cases, exceptions, or ambiguous fact patterns and explains the resulting problem; score 0 when it discusses only a simple typical case.
proposals.rationale: R05, R16, R26, and R48 expose ambiguity through contingent payments, vehicle definitions, document errors, or distinct pilot activities, unlike R04 and R29.

proposals.name: Grounded Affected-Party Knowledge
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment uses specific firsthand, professional, or organizational experience to illuminate how the proposal operates for affected people or entities; score 0 when it relies only on an affiliation label or generalized identity claim.
proposals.rationale: R08, R31, R39, R52, and R58 connect organizational experience to concrete aviation, medical-debt, clinical, transportation, or legal-service problems.

proposals.name: Constructive Alternative Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment proposes a workable alternative, fallback, or conditional modification and explains how it would address the identified problem; score 0 when it only asks the agency to reject or retain the proposal.
proposals.rationale: R07, R16, R32, R44, and R45 offer revised rules, separate requirements, or streamlined procedures, whereas R01 and R59 mainly request no change.

proposals.name: Scope Tailoring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment distinguishes relevant subgroups, uses, locations, risks, or operating conditions and matches regulatory treatment to those differences; score 0 when it treats all cases as identical.
proposals.rationale: R03, R16, R43, R45, and R48 argue for differentiated treatment based on engine models, bus types, fishing methods, eligibility, or pilot activities.

proposals.name: Temporal Transition Analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment considers historical changes, existing practices, phase-ins, deadlines, accumulated obligations, or evolving conditions and explains their significance; score 0 when timing and change over time are ignored.
proposals.rationale: R12, R30, R32, R50, R54, and R60 discuss historical baselines, prior submissions, transition periods, annual updates, or changing scientific and operational conditions.

proposals.name: Uncertainty and Counterargument Handling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment acknowledges relevant uncertainty, limitations, contrary evidence, or competing interpretations and explains why its position remains justified; score 0 when it is entirely categorical and unqualified.
proposals.rationale: R02, R12, R44, and R50 distinguish evidence quality, acknowledge limitations, or challenge competing interpretations, unlike the categorical claims in R17 and R59.

proposals.name: Objective-Tradeoff Analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies the proposal’s apparent objectives and weighs its recommendation against competing benefits, costs, risks, or affected interests; score 0 when it asserts a preferred position without discussing tradeoffs.
proposals.rationale: R07, R36, R44, R54, and R60 evaluate regulatory goals alongside environmental, safety, economic, administrative, or consumer effects.

proposals.name: Document production polish
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of formal letterhead, consistent pagination, professional spacing, typography, and document design; judge only visible formatting, not whether it is good or substantive.
proposals.rationale: Well-resourced organizations may produce polished documents and may also conduct stronger substantive work, making this a mixed nuisance rather than quality itself. Visible examples include R03 and R54.

proposals.name: Institutional identity claims
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit claims about organizational membership, size, longevity, official status, clients, or represented constituencies; do not judge whether those claims are favorable or relevant.
proposals.rationale: Reputation and network can affect reception while also supplying genuine domain knowledge, so the channel is mixed. Explicit identity claims appear in R17 and R60.

proposals.name: Legal citation density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of statutes, regulations, court cases, Federal Register citations, docket numbers, and formal legal cross-references; do not judge their correctness or usefulness.
proposals.rationale: Access to lawyers or regulatory specialists leaves a citation-heavy fingerprint and may also improve substantive analysis, so this is mixed. Examples include R28 and R59.

proposals.name: Quantitative evidence apparatus
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of numerical estimates, tables, charts, percentages, monetary amounts, measurements, and numbered empirical references; do not judge whether the evidence is accurate or persuasive.
proposals.rationale: Research capacity and expert assistance leave quantitative traces and can also produce genuinely better analysis, making this mixed. The fingerprint is prominent in R19 and R27.

proposals.name: Technical nomenclature density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of specialized acronyms, model numbers, procedural labels, engineering terms, and field-specific terminology; do not judge whether the terminology demonstrates expertise or improves the comment.
proposals.rationale: Senior or professionally embedded authors are more likely to use specialized terminology and may also possess real subject expertise. This fingerprint appears in R09 and R56.

proposals.name: Template language reuse
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of repeated stock phrases, standardized introductory language, copied headings, or formulaic agency-comment wording; do not judge whether the wording is appropriate or effective.
proposals.rationale: Professional preparation, association templates, or coordinated submissions can create reusable wording without making the underlying comment substantively better. Repeated formulaic language is visible in R11 and R29.

proposals.name: Submission-artifact markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of visible forwarding headers, email metadata, file paths, attachment notices, OCR errors, scan artifacts, or conversion defects; do not judge whether the artifacts help or hurt readability.
proposals.rationale: Document conversion, forwarding, and docket-ingestion processes leave textual artifacts unrelated to substantive content. Such markers occur in R07 and R24.

proposals.name: Attachment-and-cover framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of cover-note language that points to an attached letter, appended comments, exhibits, or separately submitted materials; do not judge whether the attached material is substantial or relevant.
proposals.rationale: Last-minute filing or multi-document submission practices can produce sparse cover text and attachment references without reflecting comment quality. Examples include R02 and R39.

proposals.name: Deadline and urgency language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit references to comment deadlines, short comment periods, expedited action, prompt consideration, or timing pressure; do not judge whether the urgency is justified.
proposals.rationale: Timing of production and filing can leave urgency fingerprints that are unrelated to the substance of the position. This appears in R11 and R30.

proposals.name: Mobilization and emotional rhetoric
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of exhortations, collective-action language, personal indignation, alarm, praise, or emotionally charged appeals; do not judge whether the tone is appropriate, sincere, or substantively meritorious.
proposals.rationale: Campaign activity and organizational mobilization can shape rhetorical intensity, while personal salience may also contribute to genuine substantive insight; therefore this is mixed. The fingerprint is visible in R05 and R27.
